open_points.subject: A19
open_points.text: the limit and every byte this rule counts are the file part's, never the form's framing. Its declared length is the request's declared length less the head read before the file — at most the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` constant, which the code that reads the head imports from the data provider (SPEC_STANDARD §15.3.1) — and the closing delimiter
open_points.question: Which exact bytes belong to the file, the head and the closing delimiter, including the CRLF immediately before the closing boundary and the CRLF after it?
options: The CRLF before the closing boundary is framing and is subtracted with the closing delimiter.
The CRLF before the closing boundary is part of the file and counts toward the file limit.
A canonical byte-level multipart grammar defines all three ranges explicitly.
open_points.default_guess: Treat the CRLF that introduces the closing boundary, the boundary line and its terminating CRLF as framing, not file bytes.

witness.initial: The import is open and an owner session has no uploaded file.
events: The owner uploads multipart data whose payload excluding the CRLF before the closing boundary is exactly 52428800 bytes.
Registry derives the file's declared length and applies the size rule.
outcomes: Registry treats that CRLF as framing and accepts the exactly-at-limit file.
Registry treats those two bytes as file data and refuses the upload as over the limit.
witness.observer: The owner sees either a mapping or an oversized-upload refusal.

open_points.subject: A19
open_points.text: the head read before the file — at most the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` constant
open_points.question: Does the constant limit all pre-file bytes consumed, the largest buffer retained while parsing them, or only the canonical form head, and exactly what must Registry do when the limit is reached before the file begins?
options: Refuse as soon as one more pre-file byte would be consumed.
Permit a longer head when it can be parsed incrementally within a bounded buffer.
Refuse only after determining that the file part cannot begin within the limit.
open_points.default_guess: Limit the total multipart-body bytes before the first file-content byte and refuse upon the first excess byte.

witness.initial: The import is open and the owner is signed in.
events: A caller sends a valid CSRF part padded with multipart headers or field data so that the file begins after `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES`.
Registry searches for and parses the file part.
outcomes: Registry refuses before reaching the file because the total head exceeds the constant.
Registry streams the long head through a bounded buffer and accepts the file because retained memory never exceeds the constant.
witness.observer: The caller sees refusal versus an accepted upload, and the owner may see a mapping in the latter case.

open_points.subject: A19
open_points.text: The upload is the file the owner interface's form sends as the second part of a multipart body, after the field that carries the CSRF value
open_points.question: Is this only a description of the owner interface's canonical request, or an acceptance rule requiring exactly one CSRF part first, exactly one file part second and no later parts; how are duplicate, reordered, unknown or trailing parts handled?
options: Accept only the exact two-part shape and refuse every deviation.
Accept any multipart body from which one valid CSRF value and one file can be selected.
Require CSRF before the file but ignore additional parts after the file.
open_points.default_guess: Require exactly the CSRF part followed by exactly one file part and then the closing boundary; refuse duplicates, reordering and extra parts.

witness.initial: The import is open and the owner has an authenticated session.
events: The owner submits a multipart request containing a valid CSRF part first, a valid file second and an extra text part third.
outcomes: Registry refuses because the body is not the specified two-part form.
Registry ignores the extra part and accepts the file.
witness.observer: The owner sees refusal versus the import mapping.

open_points.subject: A19
open_points.text: Its declared length is the request's declared length less the head read before the file — at most the imported `UPLOAD_FORM_HEAD_MAX_BYTES` constant, which the code that reads the head imports from the data provider (SPEC_STANDARD §15.3.1) — and the closing delimiter
open_points.question: What exactly is the request's declared length—an HTTP `Content-Length` value, a framework-provided decoded-body length or another value—and how is it represented when transfer coding is used or no single length exists?
options: Use the validated HTTP `Content-Length` of the encoded multipart body; absence means no declared file length.
Use the framework's decoded request-body length after transfer decoding.
Reject requests using transfer coding or otherwise lacking one valid body length.
open_points.default_guess: Use one syntactically valid HTTP `Content-Length` for the multipart body; if it is absent, perform no declared-length precheck and enforce the limit while streaming the file part.

open_points.subject: A19
open_points.text: a declared length over the limit is refused before any byte is read; otherwise Registry reads the upload up to one byte more than the limit and refuses it as soon as it holds more than the limit, whatever length was declared or whether one was
open_points.question: Besides the size check, what must happen when the declared request length is invalid, yields a negative file length, ends before the closing delimiter, or disagrees with the bytes actually delivered, and which of these cases count as an unreadable upload?
options: Refuse every malformed or inconsistent declaration and retain the previous session upload.
Ignore an unusable declaration and decide solely from the streamed multipart body.
Let the HTTP server or framework decide these cases, with no Registry-level outcome guaranteed.
open_points.default_guess: Refuse every malformed, negative, truncated or framing-inconsistent request as unreadable, retaining the session's previous upload; use streaming only when the length is valid or absent.

witness.initial: The import is open and the session already keeps file A.
events: The owner sends file B with a request length too small to include its multipart closing delimiter.
Registry receives the body and handles the inconsistent declaration.
outcomes: Registry refuses the request as unreadable and continues to keep file A.
Registry ignores the unusable declaration, parses the delivered body and replaces file A with file B.
witness.observer: The owner sees refusal versus a mapping for file B, and a later confirmation uses a different retained file.

open_points.subject: A21
open_points.text: the head before it is bounded by a constant and never kept
open_points.question: What does “never kept” forbid: durable or session retention only, retention after upload processing, or even temporary buffering required while parsing and validating the CSRF part and multipart headers?
options: The head may exist transiently during the request but must be discarded before the request completes and never enter session or durable state.
No complete head may ever be buffered; it must be parsed incrementally and discarded byte by byte.
Only durable storage is forbidden; the head may remain in process memory with the session or request objects.
open_points.default_guess: Permit bounded transient parsing memory, then discard the head before completing the request; never attach it to the owner session, logs or durable storage.

witness.initial: The import is open and the owner uploads a valid canonical multipart body.
events: Registry reads and validates the CSRF part and file headers.
The upload completes and its file is retained in the owner session.
outcomes: Registry discards all head bytes when parsing completes and retains only the file.
Registry retains the parsed or raw multipart head in the session or request object because A19 only expressly says that a refused upload is kept nowhere.
witness.observer: An operator inspecting process memory or a diagnostic dump sees whether the multipart head remains after the request.
